en: [Śrīḥ] [Vṛttaratnākaraḥ] First Chapter.

Having bowed to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, who is worshipped by Brahmā and Acyuta, and who is accompanied by Gaurī and Vināyaka, for the sake of accomplishing a continuous stream of happiness; KedV_1.1.
There was one Pavyeka, who knew the meaning of the Vedas and the Śaiva scriptures, and who brought welfare to the world;
he had a son named Kedāra, who was devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet. (Kedāra-khaṇḍa 1.2)
Therefore, this prosody (chandas), endowed with both examples and definitions, is composed under the title *Vṛttaratnākara* for the easy accomplishment of beginners. (KedV 1.3)
That which was taught by the teachers Piṅgala and others as worldly prosody (chandas) is twofold, distinguished by measure (mātrā) and syllable (varṇa); that is described here.
The extent of this Veda, which is clearly composed of six chapters,
should also be known to be one hundred and thirty-six [verses].
By these ten syllables— mya-ra-sta-ja-bh-na-ga-lā—
all that consists of speech is pervaded, just as the three worlds are pervaded by Viṣṇu.

In this [system], there are eight three-syllable groups (gaṇas): the all-heavy (sss), those with a 'la' at the end (sll), those with a 'ya' at the beginning (lyl), those with a 'ra' in the middle (ryr), those with a 'ta' at the end (str), those with a 'sa' at the beginning (sts), those with a 'ga' in the middle (gmg), and those with a 'ja' at the beginning (jja), followed by 'ja' and 'ma' (jjm). Thus, there are eight triads.

In this [meter], the groups (gaṇas) consisting of four mātrās, which are heavy at the end, middle, or beginning, and accompanied by four light syllables, are established in the Āryā and other meters. KedV_1.8 //

That [syllable] which has an anusvāra, ends in a visarga, is long, or is followed by a conjunct consonant, is to be known as *g-vakra* (curved) when it occurs at the end of a quarter-verse; otherwise, it is *mātrika* (single-mora) and *lṛju* (straight).
In this [system], the conjunction of a phoneme at the beginning of a foot is designated as "krama";
by virtue of that preceding [consonant], even a heavy syllable may sometimes become light.
O beautiful one, with little expense, the country folk enjoy young mustard greens, fresh rice, and thick curds mixed with sweets. (KedV 1.11)
The designations for the oceans, the elements, the tastes, and so forth, are to be understood according to worldly convention.
A quarter is to be known as a fourth part; a pause is designated by the term "caesura" (yati).
The wise declare that the positions of meters are even (yuk), uneven (viṣama), and mixed (ālūka);
likewise, there are even (sama), half-even (ardhasama), and uneven (viṣama) meters. (Kedavata 1.13)
Those who know the truth of the science of prosody declare that a meter is "even" (sama) when its four quarters are marked by identical characteristics. (KedV 1.14)
If the third foot of a verse is identical to the first,
and the second is like the fourth, that meter is called *ardhasama* (half-equal).
Those who are experts in the science of prosody call that a "Viṣama" (irregular) meter in which the characteristic mark differs from one to another even within the four quarters.
Starting from a single-syllable quarter-verse, with each successive quarter-verse increased by one syllable,
there arise distinct meters until the twenty-sixth [syllable] is reached.
Beyond that, the Caṇḍavṛṣṭipraghoṣa and other daṇḍakas are proclaimed;
the remainder are characterized by three or six feet per verse.
The Uktā, the Atyuktā, and likewise the Madhyā, the Pratiṣṭhā, and another preceded by the Su-; [these are] Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. KedV_1.19 //
The Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī are likewise considered, as well as the Atijagatī;
the Śakvarī should be preceded by "ati," and thereafter the Aṣṭi and the Atyaṣṭi are recorded.
Dhṛti, Atidhṛti, Kṛti, Prakṛti, Ākṛti,
Vikṛti, Saṅkṛti, as well as Atikṛti and Utkṛti.
Having thus stated the names of the meters, I shall now describe in order the characteristics of all prosodic feet (vṛtta), beginning with those measured by syllabic instants (mātrāvṛtta).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Designation of Technical Terms," in the *Vṛttaratnākara* composed by the venerable Kedārabhaṭṭa.
Chapter Two:
The Section on Āryā (1–7)

O Lakṣmī, this Āryā consists of seven gaṇas followed by a long syllable (guru), and there is no *ja* (short-long-short) gaṇa here in the odd positions; furthermore, in the first half-verse of the Āryā, the sixth gaṇa must invariably be either *na* (long-long) or *la* (short).
In the sixth [syllable], there is a restriction on the placement of the pause (yati) after the second *la* and from the first *la*;
in the final half-verse, there are five [consonants] following that, and thus here the sixth syllable becomes a *la*.
That [meter] in which a foot is seen in the first three quarters is proclaimed by the King of Nagas as having the name "Pathyā."

When the first group of three [mātrās] is elided and there is a foot consisting of two groups [of four mātrās each], Piṅgalanāga calls that *vipulā*. (Note: "saṃlaṅghya" means "having elided [the nasalized 'saṃ' or the anunāsika]").
If there are two *ja*s in both halves, with the second and fourth [syllables] situated between two *ga*s,
its name is proclaimed as *capalā* by the King of Serpents.

That [meter] whose first foot possesses all the characteristics found in the *capalā* meter, while the remaining feet possess the characteristics of the preceding [meter], was called *mukhacapalā* by the Sage. (KedV 2.6)
When the previously explained definition of the *capalā* meter is applied to the first half-verse and the other (second) half-verse,
it is called *jaghanacapalā* by those of pure intellect.
[The Section on Gīti (8–11)] If the characteristics described for the two halves of the Āryā should somehow occur in both [halves],
that Gīti, which bestows great beauty upon the two halves, was sung by the Lord of Serpents. KedV_2.8 //
If the characteristic described in the first half-verse of the Āryā applies to both halves as well, the Sage calls that an Upagīti.
That [verse] in which two noble (āryā) quarters are arranged in reverse order is indeed called an udgīti; likewise, it is joined with a division of the parts of the yati. KedV_2.10 //
If the first half of the Āryā is joined at its conclusion with one additional long syllable, and the other half is entirely like that [first half], this is called the Āryāgīti. (KedV 2.11)
[Vaitālīya Section (12–20)] There are six *kalās* in the odd [pādas] and eight in the even; and in the even [pādas], those *kalās* must not be contiguous.

Here, in the Vaitālīya, a *kalā* does not consist of two short syllables (*samā*) followed by another [short syllable] (*parāśritā*). At the end, there is a *ra* (short syllable), a *la* (short syllable), and a long syllable (*guru*).
With *ry* at the end, the remainder is likewise called *aupacchandasika* by the wise. (Kedavata 2.13)
This Āpātalikā has been described; now follows the Bhādgurukā, and the rest is as before.
The third syllable of each quarter is long, and in all feet, the second syllable is short.
In the odd quarters, the second *la* should be joined with the following syllable, which follows the northern tradition (*udīcyavṛtti*).
Then, joined with the preceding [note], the fifth is called the eastern mode (prācyavṛtti) in the two pairs.
When the even and odd feet are identical to those of the preceding two, that is the *pravṛttaka* metre.
Another variety of Aparāntikā is composed with pairs [of syllables].
She who appears alternately, possessing a beautiful smile.
[The Section on Vaktra (21–30):
That which is known as *vaktra* in the *anuṣṭubh* meter consists of four feet, each containing twelve syllables. KedV_2.21 //
The Pathyāvaktra metre is proclaimed to consist of two yugas (four gaṇas) and a ra-gaṇa (j), followed by a saridbhṛt (seven mātrās).
By the *ojayorja* [mantra], that very same [result] is obtained from the ocean; by the reverse [order] and so forth, it is the opposite.
The letter *na* is at the mouth of Capalā, and it is the ocean of the two uneven [feet].
That [verse] in which *la* is the seventh [syllable] in the even [pādas] is considered *yugmavipulā*.
The Sautrāmaṇī [rite] is performed in all [these cases] as well.
The Vipulā metre consists of eight, twelve, and eleven syllables [in its pādas].
In this manner, the others [are derived] from the fourth. KedV 2.28.
If it were not from the ocean, it would not be so vast.
The other [perception] would be preceded by that [non-perception]. (KedV 2.30)
[The Section on Mātrāsamaka (31–38):
It is called *dviguṇitavasulaghuracaladhṛti*.
Mātrāsamaka consists of nine syllables, ending with a short (l) and a long (g) syllable.
He who is the fame of the ocean of the Nīlāvarta mountain.
From that pair, Vānavāsikā may arise.
If it is adorned with five, eight, and nine [syllables], [it is the Vasantatilakā].
The Upacitrā [jagatī] occurs when nine syllables are joined with the subsequent [pāda].

That which is composed of quarters such as *mātrāsamaka* and others, endowed with various characteristics produced by past practice, and joined with an unrestricted metrical measure, is celebrated in the worlds as *pādākulaka*. (KedV 2.37)
In a *vṛtta*, the number of *ganas* is determined by the syllables; likewise, the number of syllables is determined by the *gurus*.
And the number of *gurus* is always determined by the *las* (short syllables) in a *dala*; this is the established rule.
This entire [meter] consists of ten short syllables multiplied by three (thirty), with another pair of short syllables removed;
it becomes the *śikhā* when every pair of syllables is followed by a long syllable, forming a series of feet that are beautifully composed and well-joined. *Kedāra-vyākaraṇa* 2.39.

This *khajā* meter, which brings delight to the ear and possesses a collection of qualities fashioned by a series of feet formed from pairs of syllables arranged through permutation, becomes [the *khajā*] when the letter *ña* (ñi) arrives at the head of *ja*. (KedV 2.40)
That [meter] in which eight syllables are doubled in the second half-verse is called Anaṅgakrīḍā;
furthermore, another variety composed by the poet consists of a sequence of feet where the light syllable is multiplied by eight (the oceans).
Having a body formed by two feet (syllables) consisting of three gaṇas, nine laghus, and a guru at the end, it is exceedingly beautiful.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on Mātrāvṛtta," in this commentary on the *Vṛttaratnākara* composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara.
Chapter Three.
The letter *gu* is the goddess Śrī.
The cow is the woman. // KedV_3.2 //
She is indeed a woman. // KedV 3.3 //
The female deer. // KedV_3.4 //
If there is a *mga*, it is a girl.
The *giti* consists of five *mātrās*. KedV_3.6 //
There stand those two slender-waisted women.
Śaśivadanā consists of the gaṇas nya and ya.
The streak of lightning is "mo maḥ. (Kedavata 3.9)
And if that earth [is so]. // KedV_3.10 //
If there are the ganas ma-sa-u-ga, it is Madalekhā.
The *citrapadā* metre consists of the syllables *bha*, *u*, and *ga*, with a *ga* at the end.
Mo mo go go vidyunmālā. (Kedava Tantra 3.13)
They cooked the young brahmin boy.
With the *ma*, *na*, *u*, *ga*, and *u* [mātrās], this is the cry of the swan (*haṃsaruta*).
In the *rju* [mātrā] there is the *samānikā*, and also in the *gala*.
In the *pramāṇikā* meter, there is a *ja* (jagaṇa) and a *la* (laghu) in the odd positions.
Whatever else besides these two is a canopy.
Here, the plow-faced one [is] with Rāma.
May the one who bears the infant serpent protect us both.
This is considered to be the Śuddhavirāṭ metre, consisting of the gaṇas ma, sa, ja, and ga.
If there are *ma*, *na*, *ja*, and *ga*, it is named *paṇava*.
In the *r̥ṣabha* (*ragau*) [scale], there is the *mayūrasāriṇī* [jāti]. KedV_3.23 //
In the Bhauma [yantra], joined with the Sa-ga, it is the Rukmavatīya.
The *mattā* should be known as being joined with *ma*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ga*.
She becomes as delightful as a woman, a cow, or the earth.
O friend, this [knowledge] has been presented by the Guru.
It would be Indravajrā if it has ta, ja, ga, and two gas.
Upendravajrā consists of ja, ta, ja, followed by two ga-s. KedV 3.29.
From whose feet these *upajāti* meters have been born.
In their successive births, they remember this very name of mine.
The fair-faced one was thus addressed by Najajalaga.
This is the Dodhaka meter, consisting of the syllables bha, bha, bha, and ga, followed by two short syllables (g).
The Śālinī metre is said to consist of the gaṇas ma, ta, ta, ga, and two gurus, with pauses at the fourth, seventh, and tenth syllables.
This [meter] is called Vātormī when it consists of the syllables ma, bha, ta, ga, and ga.
With five, six, seven, nine, and eight syllables, there is the Śrī [meter].
The meter Bhramaravilasita consists of the syllables ma, bha, na, la, la, and a long syllable (ga).
In this [meter], *rathoddhatā* consists of two *ra*s (two long syllables), followed by a *la* (a short syllable) and a *ga* (a long syllable).
"Welcome"—thus, from the *raṇabha* [syllables], there is a pair of heavy syllables (*guruyugma*). (KedV 3.39)
The stalks are composed of various gems and are heavy.
And Bhadrikā is characterized by moderate passion, dullness, and heaviness.
Śyenikā consists of ra, ja, ra, la, and a guru at the end of the pāda.
If there is a pearl necklace (mauktikamālā) with the ganas bha, ta, na, and ga. (Kedavata 3.43)
This [syllable] jsau, with the letter *t* and the letter *g*, is present here.
They call it the lunar path because of its reddish-white luster.
But when the sequence is ja-ta-ja-ra, it is declared to be Vaṃśastha.
Indravaṃśā may consist of eleven syllables, with the sixth and seventh being long (rasa).
In this context, the *toṭaka* meter is celebrated as consisting of four *sagaṇas*.
He states that the *drutavilambita* meter consists of the syllables na, bha, ra, and ra.
This is the Puṭa [mudrā], with the fingers of the left hand extended and those of the right hand bent. // KedV_3.50 //
And may we both have joyful faces.
The two *nyas*, accompanied by *naya*, are the *kusumavicitrā*.
With the *rasas* [of the feet] as *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *sa*, it is the *jaloddhatagati* metre.
Recite the four *gaṇas* as a string of pearls.
The *bhujaṅgaprayāta* meter consists of four [feet] of twelve syllables each.
When joined with four *ra* syllables, it is considered to be the *sragviṇī* meter.
On earth, she shall be known as Priyaṃvadā by virtue of her [syllables] na, bha, ja, and ra.
In every place, garlands of jewels were torn apart by the mouths of Guha.
The wise have declared that the *lalitā* meter consists of the syllabic feet *ta*, *bha*, *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*.
The *pramitākṣarā* meter is said to consist of the gaṇas *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *sa*.
Accompanied by the burden of the "na" syllable, she is honored and radiant.
The two Vaiśvadevī measures were indeed cut by five horses.
A garland of clouds consists of eight syllables; it is formed by the sequence *mbhau smau*.
In this [meter], Navamālikā consists of the gaṇas na, ja, bha, ya, and two i-gaṇas (i.e., two shorts followed by a long).
Prabhā consists of na-na-rau, with a pause after the fifth syllable.
In the case of the *najāvaḥ* [meter], it consists of *ma*, *la*, *ta*, *ja*, *ra*, and *u*. (KedV 3.66)
The syllables ja, bha, ja, ra, and u denote the *pañcāmara* meter.
The [meter] *abhinavatāmarasa* consists of the syllables *na*, *ja*, *ja*, and so forth.
The *nau* (na, au) meters consist of *ta*, *ra*, *sa*, *ya*, *ti*, *ta*, *ta*, and *ga*; the *kṣamā* meter consists of *ta*, *ta*, *ta*, *ga*, *sa*, *ma*.
When there are *ma*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, and *ga*, with ten syllables in each quarter, it is the *praharṣiṇī* meter.
The meter Jabhasjaga consists of four groups of four syllables and is exceedingly beautiful.
The *mattamayūra* consists of the syllables ma, ta, ya, sa, and ga, with pauses at the fourth and seventh syllables.
If this [syllable] jsau or tsau is followed by a heavy syllable (guruka), [it is called a "heavy-short"]. // KedV_3.73 //
When *sa*, *ja*, and *sa* occur, it is called *mañjubhāṣiṇī*.
By nine hundred and seventy-four years of the moon.
The *m*, *t*, *n*, *s*, *au*, *g*, *v*, *a*, *kṣa*, *gra*, *ha*, *vi*, *ra*, *ti*, *sa*, and *mbā* are the obstructed [syllables].
The Aparājitā [meter] consists of short syllables with internal pauses at the fifth and seventh [syllables].
With the gaṇas na-na-bha-na-la-gu, it is called the Praharaṇakalitā.
The Vasantatilakā meter is said to have the syllabic sequence ta, bha, ja, ja, ga, and ga.
This Siṃhonnata [stūpa] was joyfully erected by the sage Kāśyapa.
This [verse] is Uddharṣiṇī, delighted by the sage Saitava.
The moon-faced one [is described] by means of six *bhaja* gaṇas followed by a pair of *saguru* (long) syllables.
If, in a quarter-verse, there are two sets of seven *chidalolā* gaṇas (m, s, m, b, h, g, g), it is [the meter] Caraṇa.
The *gīti* meter consists of two *haya* gaṇas, one *laghu*, and a *ratha* gaṇa; it is like a digit of the moon.
This sequence of nine consonants becomes the "garland" (sraj).
In this world, the collection of the qualities of jewels is surpassed by the horse Vasuhaya.
This Mālinī is joined with the syllables *na-na-ma-ya-ya* by the worlds of the serpents.
When the ganas na, ja, bha, ja, and two rasas (six mātrās) follow, it is Prabhadraka.
That noble lady, whose gait was like that of a female elephant, led him away.
The letters *mrau* and *myau* should be joined with seven or eight crescent-moon strokes (*candralekhā*).
The *Ṛṣabhagajavilasita* meter consists of seven, three, and seven syllables [per foot], starting from a vowel (svarāt).
The Vāṇinī meter always consists of the gaṇas na, ja, bha, ja, ra, followed by a ga and a yati.
Śikhariṇī consists of [the ganas] ya, ma, na, sa, bha, la, and a long syllable (ga), with caesuras at the sixth and eleventh syllables.
The *pṛthvī* meter consists of the sequence ja-sa-ja-sa-ya-la, with eight syllables per foot and a caesura after the seventh syllable; the final syllable is long (*guru*).
The *diṅmuni* meter consists of the sequence of syllables *bha-ra-na-bha-na-la-ga*, as in the *vaṃśapatrapatita*.
When the sequence consists of ra, sa, ma, ra, sa, la, ga, and another ga, accompanied by six, two, and four syllables respectively, it is then called Hariṇī.
If the *mandākrāntā* meter consists of [the sequence] ma-bha-na-ta-ta-ga-ga, with six and four *gaṇas* from the oceans (four) and the seasons (six), it is so defined.
Narkuṭaka consists of seven, ten, and five syllables, with the *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *la*, and *guru* gaṇas.
O Sage, declare that the *kokilaka* metre consists of the syllables *ka*, *ra*, *ma*, *va*, and *i*.
The Kusumitalatāvellitā meter consists of the ganas ma, ta, na, ya, ya, with a total of thirty-two syllables (bhūta, ṛtu, aśva).
The Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre consists of twelve syllables, with the sequence ma-sa-ja-sa-ta, followed by a heavy syllable (guru).
The *suvadanā* meter is to be known as consisting of seven *gaṇas* of four syllables each, followed by six *ma-gaṇas*, a *ra-gaṇa*, and two *ya-gaṇas*, with a *bhagaṇa* at the end.
With three *ra*, *ja*, and *ga* [in each quarter], by such a characteristic, it is the name of a meter (*vṛtta*).
This *sragdharā* is proclaimed as consisting of three *mra*, *bha*, *na*, and *ri* gaṇas, joined with the three-fold restraint (*trimuniyati*) of the sages.
"Bhrau," "nara-nā-ra-nā-vatha," and "guru" [constituting] ten, twelve, and eight [mātrās] respectively, indeed form the auspicious Bhadraka metre.
If there are *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga* here, with thirty-one syllables in a quarter, then it is the *aśvalalita* metre.
The *matākrīḍā* consists of the sequence *mau, tnau, nau, na, l, g*; it is joined with eight, five, ten, and four [mātrās].
If the *tanvī* [meter] occurs here with the syllable sequence *bha-ta-na-s-bha-bha-na-ya*, it is called *bhūtamuninairyāyitī*.
In the *krauñcapada* meter, there are *bha*, *ma*, *u*, *sa*, *na*, *na*, *na*, and *ga*; here, the pauses occur at the sixth, seventh, fifth, fifth, seventh, and seventh syllables.
The *Bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita* meter consists of the ganas *vasu*, *īśa*, *aśva*, and *chada*, followed by the syllables *na*, *ma*, *ta*, *na*, *yu*, *ga*, *na*, *ra*, *sa*, and *la*.
If there are six *mo*s, *nā*s, and *ṣa*s, followed by *sa*, *ga*, and *gi*, and it is joined with nine, six, five, and three *ya*s, it is called *apavāha*.
If there are two *nayuga* (four *na*s) followed by seven *repha*s, then it becomes the *daṇḍaka* meter called *caṇḍavṛṣṭiprapāta*.
With the letter *ra* increased by a following vowel (*praticaraṇa*), there arise names such as Ṇārṇava, Vyāla, Jīmūta, Līlākara, Uddāma, Śaṅkha, and others.
That which is called *pracitaka* by those of steady intellect is known as *daṇḍaka* when it consists of seven *ya*-gaṇas followed by two *na*-gaṇas.
Thus ends the third chapter, on Even Meters (*samavṛtta*), in this commentary on the *Vṛttaratnākara* composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara.
Chapter Four.
If there is *sa*, *la*, and *ga* in the odd quarters, and *bha*, *bha*, *ra*, and two *gurus* in the even quarters, it is the *upacitra* metre.
If the first three feet contain the *ojas* (odd) gaṇas and the even feet have *na*, *ja*, and *ya*, it is *drutamadhyā*.
If there is a guru in the uneven [pādas] at the beginning of the pair of yugas, it is Vegavatī; if there are two gurus in the even [pādas], it is Bhādgau.

If there is a heavy syllable (guru) at the odd positions (ojas), namely the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth, while the first, third, fifth, and seventh are light (jagaṇa), it is Bhadravirāj; this occurs when the even positions (an-ogas) are not as specified.
In the Asama metre, there is a *sa*, a *ja*, and a *ga* followed by a heavy syllable (*guru*); in the Ketumatī metre, there is a *sa* and a *ma* followed by a *na*, a *ga*, and a *ga*.
If there is *ga*, *ja*, *ta*, *va*, *na*, *ja*, *ga*, and *ru* in the odd quarters, and *ga*, *ja*, *ta*, *va*, *na*, *ja*, *ga*, and *ru* in the even quarters, they call it *ākhyānakī*.
In the Jatau meter, if there are ja, ta, and two gas in the odd positions, and ta, ta, ja, and two gas in the even positions, this is called Viparītapūrvā.

In the *hariṇaplutā* metre, there is a light syllable at the end of each pair of quarters, a heavy syllable in the odd positions, and the sequence "na-bha-bha-ra-ka" (light-heavy-heavy-light-heavy-light) in the even positions.
The *apavaktra* meter consists of this: na, ra, la, la, and a heavy syllable (guru) in the odd quarters, and ja, ra, sa, ma, ja, and na in the even quarters. Thus, it is *jarau*. 4.9.
When there is no *yuga* (ya) following *na*, *ra*, and *pha*; and when there is *yuja* (ya) following *na*, *ja*, *ja*, *ra*, and *ga*, it is *puṣpitāgrā*.
The learned call this *vaitālīya* by the name *aparavaktra*;
some likewise designate it as *puṣpitāgrā* or *aupacchandasika*.
If there are two *ra*s in the odd positions and two *ja*s and one *ra* in the even positions, followed by a *gu*, this is the *matī* meter after the *yavā*.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the Half-Equal [Meters] in the commentary on the *Vṛttaratnākara*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara.
[The Fifth Chapter]
[The Section on *Padacaturūrdhva* (1–5):
The opening consists of eight syllables; thereafter, the quarters should be successively increased by four syllables each.
That meter which possesses a constant beauty through its various feet is called *padacaturūrdhva* by those of pure intellect. (KedV 5.1)
In which the first *mudita* (joyful) *vṛtta* possesses composed uneven feet.

When there is a pair of heavy syllables at the end of a quarter-verse, followed by a long syllable (āṅ), and a sequence of light syllables with pauses at every foot, it is called *pīḍa*. // KedV_5.2 //
If the first foot possesses a mark produced by the other [feet],
and if the second foot likewise possesses a mark from the others, and the pair of feet [the third and fourth] possess the fourth [mark], that is the *kalikā* meter. (KedV 5.3)
The third [pāda] consists of two heavy syllables followed by a sequence of equal light syllables; furthermore, it possesses the characteristics of the first and second pādas.
That which possesses all these aforementioned marks here is the *lavalī*. 5.4.
If the fourth [syllable] resides in the first [foot], and the final pair of heavy syllables reside in the last foot,
while all other [syllables] are situated above [the light ones], it is called Lalitapadā.
This very thing is a stream of nectar.
[The Section on Udgatā (6–8):
Udgatā consists of *sa*, *ja*, *ādi* (two *ga*s), *sa*, *la*, *ghu* (*ga*), and *ca*; then *na*, *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, and *ru* (*ga*).
One should recite one foot as *bha*, *na*, *ja*, *la*, *ga*, followed by *ya*, and *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *a*, *ga*. KedV_5.6 //

If all three quarters possess the characteristic of rising and falling [in the sequence], it is the Saurabhaka; provided that in this case, there are two *nagaṇas* and a *bhagaṇa* in the third quarter.
If the third foot consists of *na*, *ya*, *ga*, and a pair of *sa*s,
it is called *lalita* by those of great intelligence, provided that the remaining [feet] are indeed equal to the preceding one.

[The Section on Upasthitapracupita (9–11): When the first foot consists of the gaṇas *ms*, *jbh*, and *g* (one long syllable), and the other three feet are each different—consisting of *san*, *ja*, *ra*, and *g*—followed by *na*, *na*, and *s*, this is declared to be *Upasthitapracupita*. It is preceded by [the section on] *Upasthita*. (KedV 5.9)
In the third foot of nine syllables, with *sa* and *na*, joined by *na* and *sa*, and the first foot having *ya* and *ti*, it is called *Vardhamāna*;
the other three feet are also similar to the first; this light meter has been described here by those of expanded intellect. (KedV 5.10)
And they declare that in the first [stage], there is the state of being like a bull.
That is the Śuddhavirāṭ; if another triad standing before it were also equal to the preceding one, [it would be the same]. // KedV_5.11 //
That which has uneven syllables in its quarters, or unequal quarters like the Daśadharmaka-sūtra,
and whose meter is not specified here, is called a *gāthā* by the wise.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in this commentary on the *Vṛttaratnākara*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara.
Chapter Six.
[The Array:

The array (prastāra), the lost (naṣṭa), the indicated (uddiṣṭa), the procedure for one, two, and so forth of long and short syllables (lagakriyā), enumeration (saṅkhyāna), and the application of the path (adhvayoga)—these six are known as the auxiliary means (pratyaya). (Kedavata 6.1)
In the foot where all syllables are heavy, having placed a light syllable at the beginning beneath a heavy one,
one should perform this procedure again for the remainder as it was above.
One should add the heavy syllables to the deficient positions until all become light;
this is called "the expansion" (prastāra) by those who know the science of metrics.
When a number has been subtracted, if that which remains is even, then for each successive halving of it, there shall be a *la*.
And having placed one [syllable] on the odd positions, there should be a long syllable in each half.
[The number] has been stated.
One should write the figures (aṅka) above the first one, doubling them successively.
That [result] shall be obtained by adding one to the sum of those figures which stand in the positions of the light syllables (laghu).
[The procedure for the single and double *laghu* counts:

One should place the syllables arising from the meter, together with their respective units, arranged one above the other; and these, starting from one and so forth, should be deposited one upon the next in successive order.
One should turn back from the penultimate syllable, omitting one [syllable] at a time from above;
starting from the top, for each guru, there is the operation of one, two, and so forth, laghus.
In the collection of digits from the operation of addition, the number results from the summing of the indicated digits;
or, that sum plus one may produce this [number]. (KedV 6.8)
[The Application of the Paths]:
The wise have proclaimed that the path consists of the number itself doubled and diminished by one.
The extent of the circle should be one finger-breadth, and it should likewise extend downward by one finger-breadth.

In the lineage of Kaśyapa was born a Brahmin named Pavyeka, whose multitude of virtues was manifest, who was a knower of the Śaiva Siddhānta, and whose intellect was most pure in understanding the true meaning of the Vedas. His son was Kedāra, whose mind was one-pointedly devoted to the worship of the pair of Śiva’s feet; by him [this work] was composed, delightful through its meter.
It is called the Vṛttaratnākara (The Jewel-Mine of Metres).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the *prastāra*, in this commentary on the *Vṛttaratnākara* composed by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭarāmeśvara.
